To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
red blood cells inhibit activation induced cell death and oxidative damage in human peripheral blood lymphocyte.
RBCs protect activated human T lymphocytes from activation-induced cell apoptosis by reducing the prooxidant state.
RBCs reduce T-cell apoptosis by inhibiting the pro-oxidative state in activated T cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of red blood cells (RRCs) in the modulation of human peripheral blood T-cell proliferation and apoptosis.
the role of red blood cells (Rbc's) in the immune system.
the role of red cells in the regulation of T lymphocyte homeostasis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the RBCs are not just passive carriers of oxygen, but are also involved in the regulation of the immune system.
RBCs protect activated T cells against cell death by reducing oxidative stress.
RBCs are capable of modulating T cell homeostasis by inhibiting apoptosis, and this is mediated at least in part via a redox-dependent mechanism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the RBCs protect the T cells from activation induced cell death and oxidative damage.
RBCs protect activated T cells from apoptosis, at least in vitro, and that they do so by reducing the prooxidant state of T lymphocytes.
RBCs are not just passive transporters of O2, but also play an active role in protecting T cells from oxidative stress-induced cell death, thus modulating the immune response.
The main takeaway from our work is that
red blood cells (RBS), which are the most abundant cells in the human body, are able to inhibit T-cell apoptosis, at least in vitro.
RBCs protect human T cells from activation induced cell death, at the very least, partially by reducing the prooxidant state.
RBCs are capable of protecting T lymphocytes from apoptosis and oxidative stress.
